d: Break apart or in two, using violence
ety: From Middle English sundren (“to separate, part, divide”), from Old English sundrian (“to separate, split, part, divide”), from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną (“to separate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sen(e)- (“separate, without”). Cognate with Scots sinder, sunder (“to separate, divide, split up”), Dutch zonderen (“to isolate”), German sondern (“to separate”), Swedish söndra (“to divide”). More at sun
s: In Taran's hand the sundered bone had turned into gray dust, which he cast aside.

d: A spear with three or more prongs; used for spearing fish (especially salmon)
ety: From earlier leyster, lister, perhaps via Middle English *lēster, *līster, from Old Norse ljóstr (“leister”), from ljósta (“to smite, strike; to hit, strike (with an arrow or spear)”), from Proto-Germanic *leustaną (“to hit, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *lew-s- (“to loosen (by knocking)”); the word is cognate with Danish lyster (“fish spear, gig, leister”), Icelandic ljósta (“to hit, strike”
s: The shaft parts taper slightly upwards, have rounded outer surfaces and flat or slightly concave inner surfaces which are adapted to the shape of the leister pole.

d: Lacking in harmony or compatibility or appropriateness
ety: From Latin incongruus, from in- (“not”) + congruus (“congruent”), equivalent to in- + congruous.
s: 20 and 25 are incongruous with respect to 4.

d: Habitually reserved and uncommunicative
ety: Back-formation from taciturnity, from Middle English taciturnite, from Latin taciturnitās; or alternatively from French taciturne, likely reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).
s: The two sisters could hardly have been more different, one so boisterous and expressive, the other so taciturn and calm.

d: Express strong disapproval of
ety: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”) + corium (“hide, skin”) + -ō. Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern Eng
s: The teacher continued to excoriate the student after his academic issues.

d: Pathologically excessive (and often incoherent) talking
ety: From logo- (prefix meaning ‘word; speech’) + -rrhea (suffix meaning ‘flowing’), probably modelled after verbal diarrhea. logo- is derived from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word; speech; utterance”) (from λέγω (légō, “to say, speak; to arrange; to gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect, gather”)), while -rrhea is from ῥοία (rhoía, “a flow, flux”) (from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”), from Pro
s: But, then, these persons have not only a copia verborum as to knowledge, but a volubility sometimes amounting to a logorrhœa in expressing what they know—although that may not be much.

d: Adapted for grasping especially by wrapping around an object
ety: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.
s: Some monkeys have prehensile tails which they use to pick things up.

d: Someone who intrudes on the privacy or property of another without permission
ety: From inter- + loper (“runner, rover”), as in landloper (“vagrant”) (from lope (“to leap, to jump”) (originally dialectal)). Originally spelt enterloper and used in specific sense, “unauthorized trader trespassing on privileges of chartered companies”, later general sense of “self-interested intruder” from 1630s.
s: They disliked the interloper, and forced him to leave.

d: An assistant or subordinate bishop of a diocese
ety: From Anglo-Norman, Old French suffragam, from (the stem of) Latin suffrāgium (“suffrage”).
s: A suffragan could share the tasks which were special to bishops; for example, by conducting confirmations.

d: Lying on the stomach with head raised with legs pointed forward
ety: From Middle English couchant, from Middle French couchant.
s: Or again, have you ever watched fine collie dogs couchant at twenty yards' distance?

d: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of
ety: From Middle English mollifien, from Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, Latin moll- + -ify.
s: He tried to mollify the angry customer.

d: Associated by chance and not an integral part
ety: From Medieval Latin adventītius (“coming from abroad, extraneous”), a corruption of Latin adventīcius (“foreign, strange, accidental”), from adventus (“arrival, coming, approach, advent”) + -īcius (suffix forming adjectives), from adveniō (“to arrive”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns).
s: The adventitious disappearance of those nearer the throne than the duke had, moreover, set tongues awagging.

d: Stop from happening or developing
ety: The origin of the noun is uncertain; the following etymologies have been suggested: * According to Gerald Leonard Cohen, Stephen Goranson, and Matthew Little, at present the most likely derivation is as a non-rhotic variant of kurbash (“heavy whip, lash”), from Arabic كُرْبَاج (kurbāj, “lash, whip”), or from its etymon Ottoman Turkish قرباچ (kırbaç, “lash, whip”) (whence Turkish kırbaç (“whip”)).
s: Extensive highlights from Glastonbury, an Allied mission to kibosh the German A-bomb and a homage to Arthur Ashe.

d: Feelings of anxiety that make you tense and irritable
ety: From dis- + quietude.
s: The lawyer stood awhile when Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of disquietude.

d: Possessing or believed to possess magic power especially protective power
ety: From talisman + -ic.
s: For Marshall, law possessed a talismanic quality, representing all that was best in American democracy.

d: Someone who lends money at excessive rates of interest
ety: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).
s: "You can go to the Carpetbag usurers if you want money."

d: A rope for raising or lowering a sail or flag
ety: Inherited from Middle English halier, from halen (“to haul”) + -iere (“-er”), with misconstrual of -ier as yard. Compare lanyard.
s: Uncleat the black main halyard to lower and remove the jib cover; remove the main halyard from the jib cover.

d: State of disgrace resulting from public abuse
ety: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.
s: Her death I could have born, but the death of her honour has added obloquy and shame to that sorrow which bends my grey hairs to the dust!

d: Rich and superior in quality
ety: Borrowed from Latin opulēns, opulentus, from ops (“wealth, power, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op- (“to work; produce in abundance”).
s: He saw himself, in a smart suit and a songkok, bowed into the opulent suites of Ritzes and Waldorfs and baring, under dark glasses, a hairy chest to a milder sun by a snakeless sea.

d: A low continuous indistinct sound; often accompanied by movement of the lips without the production of articulate speech
ety: 1350–1400; Medieval Latin murmuratio (“murmuring, grumbling”), equivalent to murmur + -ation. The “flock of starlings” sense is probably derived from the sound of the very large groups that starlings form at dusk.
s: "Oh! I wasted most of my morning crawling to a murmuration of starlings, which I foolishly mistook for congregation of plover."

d: Of great mass; huge and bulky
ety: From Latin elephantīn(us). By surface analysis, elephant + -ine.
s: The bell rang for the end of the lesson. Overhead and all around came the elephantine sounds of hundreds of students on the move.

d: The floating wreckage of a ship
ety: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.
s: “What about that one?” “That'll do nicely. That gaggle of human flotsam doesn't even belong on the sea.”

d: Rope or canvas headgear for a horse, with a rope for leading
ety: Perhaps from Spanish jáquima (“halter”).
s: Before they could agree or disagree he’d hauled the horse around by the hackamore and was pounding off up the track.

d: Burn superficially or lightly
ety: From Middle English swengen (“to strike”), from Old English swenġan (“to dash, strike; to cause to swing”), from Proto-West Germanic *swangijan (“to cause to swing”).
s: The scorching flame fore swinged all his face

d: Light carriage; pulled by a single horse
ety: Named after British statesman Lord Brougham (1778–1868), who either invented or popularized the vehicle.
s: “Yes,” he continued, glancing out of the window. “A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties.”

d: The effect of supernatural or divine intervention in human affairs
ety: From Late Latin theūrgia, from Ancient Greek θεουργίᾱ (theourgíā, “sorcery”), from θεός (theós, “god”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, the- + -urgy.
s: Spiritual magic or theurgy was based on the idea that one could reach God in an ascent up the scale of creation made possible by a rigorous course of prayer, fasting and devotional preparation.

d: Quickly aroused to anger
ety: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.
s: I am naturally irascible, and if I could have shaken this negative gentleman vigorously, the relief would have been immense.

d: A camp defended by a circular formation of wagons
ety: From South African Dutch lager (“camp”) (modern Afrikaans laer), from German Lager, from Middle High German leger, from Old High German legar, from Proto-Germanic *legrą. Doublet of lager and lair.
s: “And for how long d'you think you're going to be safe in the cities?” Louis persisted. “Just a matter of time, then our frontiers will shrink as we draw our little laager more and more tightly.”

d: A garment resembling a tunic that was worn by men in the Middle Ages
ety: From Middle English kirtel, from Old English cyrtel, cognate with Old Norse kyrtill (“tunic”) (whence Icelandic kyrtill, Danish kjortel (“gown, tunic”), Swedish kjortel (“petticoat, skirt”)), from Old Norse *kurtil-, supposedly a diminutive of *kurt-, from Latin curtus (“short, shortened”). Compare German Kittel.
s: Many of the church dignitaries are distinguishable by peculiarities of dress, as the shovel hat and kirtle.

d: A conspicuous mistake whose effects seem to reverberate
ety: From clang (“loud ringing sound”) + -er.
s: In his speech, the best man got the bride's name wrong. What a clanger!

d: Translating an idea into action
ety: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).
s: Differences between theory and praxis of communism.

d: Resembling or characteristic of a prophet or prophecy
ety: From Latin sibyllinus, Sibillinus, from Sibylla. By surface analysis, sibyl + -ine.
s: Another early form of rhapsodomancy is represented by the sibylline books.

d: Compensation received by virtue of holding an office or having employment (usually in the form of wages or fees)
ety: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.
s: Plus, the Department of Justice has argued in the past that SGEs are subject to the emoluments clause, which means they cannot take payments from foreign governments.

d: Large deep serving dish with a cover; for serving soups and stews
ety: From earlier terrene (thus pronunciations with /tj/, /t͡ʃ/ are spelling pronunciations), borrowed from French terrine. Doublet of terrine.
s: The large covered soup tureen, as well as the 15 inch round plate on which it sat, was rimmed by gold leaf, and was decorated with an ornate nineteenth century English scene.

d: An excited state of agitation
ety: Origin uncertain. Compare Dutch peuteren (“to rummage, poke”), and English potter, pudder.
s: (name of the article) Flight Of Hess Causes Pother Among Germans

d: A person who walks from place to place
ety: From French péripatétique, from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) (English peri-)+ πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).
s: He who would think clearly must think like a peripatetic even if he is unwilling to walk like one.

d: Contaminated with infecting organisms
ety: Mid 15th century, in sense “mischievous, pernicious”, from Latin pestifer (“bearing plague”), from pestis (“plague”) + -fer (“carrying”). By surface analysis, pesti- + -ferous (“bearing, carrying”).
s: In these solemn moments man discovers the germ of those vices, which like the Java tree shed a pestiferous vapour around--death is in the shade!

d: Substituting a more inclusive term for a less inclusive one or vice versa
ety: Borrowed from Latin synecdochē, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).
s: "Holocaust" can become a tired synecdoche for war crimes in general.

d: A person who is uninterested in intellectual pursuits
ety: The noun is derived from Philistine, influenced by philister, Philister (“(historical) in German universities: person not associated with the university; person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art or culture”), from German Philister (“person from ancient Philistia; (figurative, dated) person not associated with a university; (figurative) person who lacks appreciation of or is
s: They all want to know how you get to me, let them feel how they feel and be philistines because this type of love's the epitome said.

d: Spur on or encourage especially by cheers and shouts
ety: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).
s: And now, my dear sir, let me exhort you to take care of yourself.
